source.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
source.authors: Gonçalo Paulo; Alex Troy Mallen; C. Juang; Nora Belrose

page_placements.theme: Non-basis directions (SAE, sparse coding, PCA, k-means, NMF) are more monosemantic than neurons or basis dimensions

record.tranche_reason: The study refines how neuron interpretability is assessed: reported neuron interpretation scores vary with the top-k activation selection and scoring measure. It does not directly estimate how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper's main experiments concern sparse-autoencoder features and their automated interpretations. The neuron-specific results relevant here are the neuron comparisons in Table A10. Other reported score, sampling, and layer results are primarily for SAE features and are not recorded as neuron-polysemanticity results.
record.test_reason: The paper is about automated interpretation of SAE features. It invokes neuron polysemanticity only as motivation for SAEs. Its only neuron results (Table A10) are a baseline comparison of interpretation scores against its SAE features. These scores measure explanation quality, not how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs, so no version is directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it overweights a side result. The main conclusions concern SAE features. The authors propose cheaper scoring methods (fuzzing, detection, embedding, surprisal, intervention), say interpretations should be generated from the whole activation distribution, and say intervention scoring explains output features missed by context-based methods. The neuron result is secondary: neurons significantly underperform SAEs, and top-k sparsification helps only slightly.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses automated LLM-generated interpretations and fuzzing/detection scores, with neuron comparisons alongside extensive SAE-feature experiments; it does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron interpretation scores differ between top-32 and top-256 selection; the study also compares fuzzing and detection measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Automated LLM interpretations of neurons score near the random baseline. In Gemma 2 9b, fuzzing is 0.59–0.62 and detection 0.57–0.59; in Llama 3.1 8b, fuzzing is 0.54–0.55 and detection 0.53. The random baseline is 0.51 and SAE features score 0.70–0.83. Top-32 sparsification raises neuron scores only slightly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual LLM neurons are much less explainable by single automated natural-language interpretations than SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: For SAE features, interpretations depend on which activation quantiles are shown to the explainer and on the scoring method. Top-example interpretations are narrower and fail on lower deciles. Scores from different methods disagree, for example fuzzing 0.9 vs detection 0.43 for one feature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For SAE features (not neurons), whether a unit appears to have one coherent meaning depends on the activation range sampled and on the scoring method.

record.code_released: The paper says the delphi library and accompanying scripts are released, but no URL is stated in the provided text.
record.problems: The neuron-specific evidence is interpretation-score comparison, not a direct test of whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or a count of polysemantic neurons. The reported neuron table gives medians and interquartile ranges but no statistical tests for these comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Table A10's SAE-feature results were left out because they are not neuron results. The other interpretation-score and sampling results, including Tables A1–A9 and the layer analyses, are chiefly about SAE features rather than neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: There is no count or share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no layer comparison for neurons.
No test of superposition as the cause.
No test of activation function, architecture or regularization effects on neuron polysemanticity.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
The sampling and scoring-method dependence is shown only for SAE features, not neurons. There is no neuron polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: Neuron polysemanticity appears only as cited motivation in the introduction (Arora et al., Elhage et al.). Table A10 does not state the neuron site (MLP vs residual) or the layers. The reader's V7 'supports' label is dropped: the neuron top-k differences are tiny with no statistics, and the activation-range and scoring dependence is shown only for SAE features. Zoom In is cited but not tested.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and the InceptionV1 neuron example.
The study does not measure the share of language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare that share across layers.
No test of superposition as the cause of neuron polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.

The study compares neuron and SAE interpretation scores, but does not test the stated activation-function, architecture, or regularization effects on polysemantic-neuron share or the associated performance cost.
No investigation of canonical polysemantic neurons as shared features or related offshoots of one job.
The neuron results compare top-k selection and interpretation scores, but do not directly classify neurons as polysemantic or measure changes in the number or share so classified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper builds its SAE-interpretation method on neuron polysemanticity and runs neuron baselines, without testing polysemanticity. This matches T4. 'assumes' would also be defensible, but the given value is not wrong.

tranche.reason: Polysemanticity motivates the SAE method. The only neuron results are interpretation-quality baselines against SAE features in Table A10. No result measures how many neurons are polysemantic. No result argues that a version is wrong.

source_check.notes: All eight Table A10 rows match the text (explainer and scorer Llama 3.1 70b, 4-bit). The text does not state the neuron site (MLP or residual) or the layers. The scores measure explanation quality, not polysemanticity. Llama neurons score at the randomly initialized TopK SAE level. The code is released (delphi library), contrary to the pack's 'code: n'.

statements.correction: Table A10 (explainer and scorer Llama 3.1 70b). Random interpretation: fuzzing 0.51, detection 0.51. Randomly initialized TopK SAE: 0.55 fuzzing, 0.54 detection. Gemma 2 9b neurons, top 32 / top 256: fuzzing 0.62 / 0.59, detection 0.59 / 0.57. These are above random and below Gemma SAEs (0.70-0.76). Llama 3.1 8b neurons: fuzzing 0.55 / 0.54, detection 0.53 / 0.53. These are near random, at the level of the random TopK SAE. Trained SAEs: 0.70-0.83. Authors: neurons improve when sparsified to top k but still significantly underperform SAEs.
statements.problem: All numbers match Table A10, but 'near the random baseline' fits only Llama. Gemma neurons (0.57-0.62) sit about midway between random (0.51) and Gemma SAEs (0.70-0.76). The authors say only that neurons significantly underperform SAEs.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Neuron interpretation evaluations in Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b, comparing top-32 and top-256 selection
reader_labels.reason: The measured interpretation scores differ with top-k selection and are low compared with SAE feature scores, consistent with assessment depending on what is measured; the scores do not directly count polysemantic neurons.
